pages.title: Delivering Answers and Hope for Rare Disease Families | FDA
pages.description: For the U.S. Food and Drug Administration, rare diseases present both our most formidable challenge and our greatest opportunity to speed life-saving treatments and cures to the patients who need them most.
pages.text: Delivering Answers and Hope for Rare Disease Families | FDA Skip to main content Skip to FDA Search Skip to in this section menu Skip to footer links Home News & Events FDA Newsroom FDA Voices Delivering Answers and Hope for Rare Disease Families FDA Voices In this section Image By: Kyle Diamantas, J.D., Acting Commissioner of Food and Drugs As a father of three young girls, I know the fierce, protective love every parent feels for their children. Whenever one of my daughters gets sick, my instincts kick in and I want answers immediately. For millions of families across America, unfortunately those answers do not come quickly or easily. Instead, they face months or even years of uncertainty, bouncing between doctor visits while watching a loved one, often a child, battle a formidable mysterious illness. Stories like that of Baby KJ, who received the world’s first personalized CRISPR gene-editing therapy, remind us of what is truly at stake. Facing a rare, complex condition early in life, Baby KJ’s journey represents the agonizing path so many families endure. They wait for a diagnosis, search endlessly for clinical trials, and pray for a treatment that may not yet exist. Kyle Diamantas, J.D. In one of my first actions as Acting Commissioner, I convened a roundtable of rare disease advocates to familiarize myself with the concerns of the rare disease community. Department of Energy Information Quality Guidelines Information Quality The Department of Energy’s Information Quality Act Guidelines are developed in accordance with Section 515, Treasury and General Government Appropriations Act (Pub.L. 106-554). The law directed the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) to issue government-wide guidelines that "provide policy and procedural guidance to Federal Agencies for ensuring and maximizing the quality, objectivity, utility, and integrity of information (including statistical information) disseminated by Federal Agencies." OMB guidelines, published in the Federal Register on February 22, 2002 (67 FR 8452), direct agencies to issue their own implementing guidelines that include administrative mechanisms allowing members of the public to seek and obtain correction of information disseminated by the agency that does not comply with OMB or agency guidelines (available at OMB Information Quality Guidelines ). pages.description: art002e014225 (April 6, 2026) – Seen from afar, Earth appears as a small, delicate waning crescent suspended in the darkness of space, captured by the crew during the Artemis II mission. Despite its distance, faint hints of Earth’s blue tones and cloud patterns are visible, offering a striking perspective of our home planet from deep space.

Dow, X-energy Receive Construction Permit for Advanced Nuclear Project in Texas DOE-supported project becomes first advanced nuclear facility approved for construction at a U.S. industrial site. Office of Nuclear Energy November 13, 2026 Estimated Read Time min Rendering of the Dow plant in Seadrift, Texas. Courtesy of X-energy The U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) approved a construction permit on November 9 for Dow and X-energy’s proposed Long Mott Generating Station at Dow’s Seadrift Operations site in Texas. The approval marks the first advanced nuclear facility authorized for construction at a U.S. industrial site, the first NRC construction permit for a high-temperature gas-cooled reactor in more than 50 years, and the first-ever NRC approval for a pebble-bed core design. This project is supported by the U.S. Department of Energy’s (DOE) Advanced Reactor Demonstration Program , which aims to accelerate commercial deployment of advanced nuclear reactor technologies in the United States. Not all fish, shellfish, or the insects that they eat can tolerate the same amount of acid. An ecosystem is a community of plants, animals and other organisms along with their environment including the air, water and soil. Everything in an ecosystem is connected. If something harms one part of an ecosystem – one species of plant or animal, the soil or the water – it can have an impact on everything else. Effects of Acid Rain on Fish and Wildlife The ecological effects of acid rain are most clearly seen in aquatic environments, such as streams, lakes, and marshes where it can be harmful to fish and other wildlife. As it flows through the soil, acidic rain water can leach aluminum from soil clay particles and then flow into streams and lakes. Skip to global NPS navigation Skip to the main content Skip to the footer section National Park Service Search Search This Site All NPS Exiting nps.gov Cancel Contact Us The Legacy of Slavery As the United States expanded from 13 colonies, the debates over chattel slavery grew—some states came to abolish it, while others refused to untangle their political, economic, and social life from the institution. With the outbreak of the Civil War in 1861, enslaved African Americans saw the war as opportunity to emancipate themselves. When President Lincoln authorized the Emancipation Proclamation, formerly enslaved African American men joined the Union army to fight for the full emancipation of their race. The conclusion of the war in Union victory and the ratification of the 13th, 14th, and 15th Amendments to the US Constitution brought African Americans closer than they ever had been to full citizenship. Nevertheless, the struggle for equality continued. Through our historical resources, the National Park Service tells these stories of African-American perseverance in the face of great adversity. pages.title: Facility Systems Safety Engineer and Fall Protection Program Administrator Thu Nguyen - NASA
pages.description: "I had two kids that were three and five, and I was working full time, and I was doing the master's program...It was tough, but I had to get it done to show my kids that anything is possible." – Thu Nguyen, Facility Systems Safety Engineer and Fall Protection Program Administrator, NASA’s Johnson Space Center
